ety.text: Old French justebor. Middle English juste English just From Middle English juste, from Old French juste, from Latin iūstus (“just, lawful, rightful, true, due, proper, moderate”), from Proto-Italic *jowestos, related to Latin iūs (“law, right”); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-. Compare Scots juist (“just”), Saterland Frisian juust (“just”), West Frisian just (“just”), Dutch juist (“just”), German Low German jüst (“jüst”), German just (“just”), Danish just (“just”), Swedish just (“just”). Doublet of giusto.
Variation of joust, presumably ultimately from Latin iuxta (“near, besides”).

senses.d: Factually right, correct; factual.
ex: It is a just assessment of the facts.

senses.d: Rationally right, correct.
Morally right; upright, righteous, equitable; fair.
ex: It looks like a just solution at first glance.

My lord, we know your grace to be a man
Just and upright.

senses.d: Proper, adequate.
Only, simply, merely.
ex: Just plant a few tomatoes, unless you can freeze or dry them.
He calls it vermilion, but it's just red to me.

senses.d: Introduces a disappointing or surprising outcome that renders futile something previously mentioned.
ex: I spent two hours cooking my favorite recipe, just to burn the rice and ruin the meal.
I helped him out, just for him to betray me.

senses.d: Used to reduce the force of an imperative; simply.
ex: Just follow the directions on the box.

senses.d: Used to increase the force of an imperative; simply, without questioning.
ex: I'm tired of playing games – just get it done.

senses.d: Used to convey a less serious or formal tone.
ex: I just called to say "hi".

senses.d: Absolutely, positively.
ex: It is just splendid!
just fine

senses.d: Moments ago, only very recently.
ex: They just left, but you may leave a message at the desk.

senses.d: By a narrow margin; closely; narrowly; almost not.
ex: The fastball just missed my head!
The fire department arrived just in time.

senses.d: Exactly, precisely, perfectly.
ex: He wants everything just right for the big day.
And having just enough, not covet more.

senses.d: Expressing dismay or discontent.
A joust, tournament.
To joust, fight a tournament.
ex: He iusts with her vnknowne whom he lou’d best, [...].

From Middle English justice, from Old French justise, justice (Modern French justice), from Latin iūstitia (“righteousness, equity”), from iūstus (“just”), from iūs (“right”), from Proto-Italic *jowos, perhaps literally "sacred formula", a word peculiar to Latin (not general Italic) that originated in the religious cults, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-. Doublet of Justitia. Partly displaced native Old English rihtwīsnes (Modern English righteousness < rightwiseness).

senses.d: Having a justification.
ex: The act was fully justified.

senses.d: Of text, arranged on a page or a computer screen such that the left and right ends of all lines within paragraphs are aligned, with the space between words adjusted as necessary. Also called fully justified to contrast with left-justified and right-justified.

grp.label: having lines arranged on a page or computer screen

ety.text: From giustific(are) (“to justify”) + -ato (1ˢᵗ conjugation past participle suffix).
Past participle of justificar.
From Middle English justifien, from Old French justifier, from Late Latin justificare (“make just”), from Latin justus, iustus (“just”) + ficare (“make”), from facere, equivalent to just + -ify.

senses.d: To provide an acceptable explanation for.
ex: How can you justify spending so much money on clothes?
Paying too much for car insurance is not justified.

senses.d: To be a good reason behind a normally-unacceptable action; to warrant.
ex: Nothing can justify your rude behaviour last night.
Preservation of two railway routes between Belfast and Derry could no longer be justified and one of them must go.

senses.d: To arrange (text) on a page or a computer screen such that the left and right ends of all lines within paragraphs are aligned.
ex: The text will look better justified.

senses.d: To absolve, and declare to be free of blame or sin.
ex: I cannot justify whom the law condemns.
And by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.

senses.d: To give reasons for one’s actions; to make an argument to prove that one is in the right.
ex: She felt no need to justify herself for deciding not to invite him.
[…] I was equally unable to justify myself and unwilling to acknowledge my errors […]

senses.d: To prove; to ratify; to confirm.
ex:
[…] say
My wife’s a hobby-horse, deserves a name
As rank as any flax-wench that puts to
Before her troth-plight: say’t and justify’t.

senses.d: To show (a person) to have had a sufficient legal reason for an act that has been made the subject of a charge or accusation.
To qualify (oneself) as a surety by taking oath to the ownership of sufficient property.
ex: J'USTIFYING BAIL, practice, is the production of bail in court, who there justify' themselves against the exception of the plaintiff.
